subject: the axolotl

real.text: The axolotl is a species of mole salamander. It is neotenic, reaching sexual maturity without undergoing metamorphosis, and the adults remain fully aquatic with obvious external gills. Axolotls may be difficult to distinguish from the larval stage of other neotenic adult mole salamanders, in particular the tiger salamander, or other species such as mudpuppies.

fake.text: The axolotl is a salamander famous for never fully leaving its larval life, staying in water its whole existence while keeping feathery external gills. Found in Mexico’s lakes and canals, it can regrow lost limbs—and even parts of its spinal cord—making it a favorite of scientists studying regeneration. Thanks to habitat loss and pollution, it’s now critically endangered, so conservation efforts are crucial for its survival.

tell: The real one opens with a dated species description; the generated one starts with a hook and never dates anything.

subject: sourdough bread

real.text: Sourdough is a leavening agent containing naturally occurring yeast and lactobacillus bacteria. The term is used to describe bread baked with sourdough, while the sourdough itself is referred to as a starter. In addition to leavening the bread, the fermentation process produces lactic acid, which gives the bread its distinctive sour taste and improves its keeping qualities.

fake.text: Sourdough bread starts with a living starter—flour and water fermented by wild yeast and bacteria. When you mix it into a dough, the starter slowly develops flavor, giving the bread a tangy taste and a chewy, open crumb. Unlike quick breads, sourdough often needs time: it ferments and proofs until the dough is airy and elastic. Baking then locks in that character, making every loaf a little different.

tell: Watch for a closing sentence that summarises. Human encyclopaedic prose rarely signs off, generated prose often does.

subject: the aurora borealis

real.text: An aurora is a natural light display in Earth's upper atmosphere caused by charged particles from the Sun colliding with atoms in the atmosphere. These collisions excite oxygen and nitrogen, which then emit light of different colours such as green, red, and purple. When observed in high-latitude regions they are called polar lights and aurora polaris. In the Arctic they are called the northern lights or aurora borealis; in the Antarctic, the term southern lights or aurora australis is used. Auroras display dynamic patterns of radiant light that appear as curtains, rays, spirals or dynamic flickers covering the entire sky.

fake.text: The aurora borealis is a colorful light show that appears in high-latitude skies near the Arctic. It happens when charged particles from the Sun stream toward Earth and collide with gases in the atmosphere. Oxygen and nitrogen glow in different colors—often green, sometimes pink or red—while magnetic fields guide the particles like invisible rails. The best views are usually on clear, dark nights during winter.

tell: Both read cleanly, so the tell is precision: the real paragraph commits to specific altitudes and particle names.

subject: the baobab tree

real.text: Adansonia is a genus of medium-to-large deciduous trees known as baobabs or boababs. The eight species of Adansonia are native to Africa, Australia, and Madagascar but have also been introduced to other regions of the world, including Barbados, where several of the baobabs there are suspected to have originated from Africa. Other baobabs have been introduced to Asia. A genomic and ecological analysis further suggests that the genus itself originated in Madagascar.

fake.text: Baobab trees are the giants of Africa’s dry landscapes, famous for their thick, water-storing trunks that can seem to “grow upside down” because of their flat, branching crowns. They’re often called the “tree of life” since they provide shade, leaves, fruit, and—when water is scarce—an emergency source of moisture. Living for centuries, baobabs grow slowly but become landmarks for wildlife and people alike.

subject: the Voyager 1 spacecraft

real.text: Voyager 1 is a space probe launched by NASA on September 5, 1977, as part of the Voyager program, to study the outer Solar System and the interstellar space beyond the Sun's heliosphere. It was launched 16 days after its twin, Voyager 2. It communicates through the NASA Deep Space Network (DSN) to receive routine commands and to transmit data to Earth. Real-time distance and velocity data are provided by NASA and JPL. At a distance of 171.19 AU as of August 2026, it is the most distant human-made object from Earth. Voyager 1 is projected to reach a distance of one light day from Earth in November 2026.

fake.text: Voyager 1 is an interplanetary spacecraft launched by NASA on 5 September 1977 to study the outer planets. It conducted close flybys of Jupiter and Saturn and later entered interstellar space, crossing the heliopause in 2012. Voyager 1 carries instruments for measuring magnetic fields, plasma, cosmic rays, and planetary atmospheres. Its power comes from a decaying radioisotope thermoelectric generator system.

tell: Numbers separate them: the real text is dense with dates, distances and instrument names that can be checked.

subject: plate tectonics

real.text: Plate tectonics is the scientific theory that Earth's lithosphere comprises a number of large tectonic plates, which have been slowly moving since 3–4 billion years ago. The model builds on the concept of continental drift, an idea developed during the first decades of the 20th century. Plate tectonics came to be accepted by geoscientists after seafloor spreading was validated in the mid- to late 1960s. The processes that result in plates and shape Earth's crust are called tectonics.

fake.text: Plate tectonics is the theory describing Earth’s lithosphere as a set of large and smaller rigid plates that move relative to one another over the more ductile asthenosphere. Plate boundaries include divergent, convergent, and transform types, associated with seafloor spreading, subduction, mountain building, earthquakes, and volcanic activity. Driving forces include mantle convection, slab pull, and ridge push, while plate motions are monitored by geodesy and paleomagnetism.

tell: Both are neutral and correct. The tell is sentence rhythm — generated prose keeps an even beat, human prose varies.
